title: Understand the Writing Task
outcome: On at least two fresh prompts, identify Topic / Task / Must Include / Boundary, distinguish subject from action, find omitted details, and save an original four-part Task Map plus Task Commitment Note.

concepts.label: Topic
concepts.caution: Topic alone is not an instruction to write an essay.

concepts.label: Task
concepts.explanation: What you have to do for the reader, such as invite, request or explain.
concepts.caution: Do not turn a request into an unrelated story.

concepts.label: Must Include
concepts.explanation: Facts and actions that the prompt explicitly requires.
concepts.caution: Interesting but unrequested details cannot replace required ones.

concepts.label: Boundary
concepts.explanation: Audience, time, setting, scope, tone or other limits.
concepts.caution: One phrase can serve more than one defensible role.

demo.instruction: Before writing, don't ask 'What can I say?' Ask 'What do I need to do for this reader?' Read the whole task.
demo.prompt: Write a friendly email to a classmate inviting them to the school art exhibition on Friday. Include the starting time and where to meet.

steps.label: Notice the action
steps.text: “Write a friendly email ... inviting” is the Task: I must invite, not review a painting.

steps.label: Identify the subject
steps.text: “School art exhibition” is the Topic: the event I must talk about.

steps.label: Check non-negotiables
steps.text: “Starting time” and “where to meet” are Must Include; “Friday” is a scheduling constraint I must respect.

steps.label: Choose for the reader
steps.text: “To a classmate” defines the Boundary: friendly but clear language.

steps.label: Reject and repair
steps.text: “I drew a beautiful picture last year” is not an invitation. A task-aligned opening could be “Would you like to come to the school art exhibition on Friday?” It still needs a starting time and meeting place.

demo.thinkQuestion: Could an email be about the right exhibition but still fail? Why?
demo.expectedConcept: Yes. It may omit the invitation, time or place.
demo.commonError: If you only identify the exhibition, look at the verbs write and inviting: what is the reader expected to do?
demo.a1: invite = ask someone to come; recipient = person who receives the message.
demo.b1: Explain why the date and meeting point affect clarity and why a classmate needs a friendly tone.

cycleA.prompt: Write a short message to your school librarian requesting longer opening hours on Saturday. Explain why students need this and suggest a closing time.
cycleA.instructions: First choose a label, then classify the six exact phrases. Keyboard: tab to the phrase label selector and press the arrow keys. After checking, write the four-part Task Map in your own words. Fixed labels are the most direct role; a phrase can have another defensible role in your own explanation.

chunks.rationale: Day constraint, not the full Topic. Its contextual role can also be defended in a free-text explanation.
The prompt explicitly requires a reason for the request.
The prompt explicitly requires a specific proposed closing time.

cycleA.clarification: The combined Topic is the school library's opening hours, not Saturday itself. The fixed-label tool checks direct labels only. Original Task Maps are never graded by keyword or exact-string matching.

fields.label: Task
fields.help: What action should my message perform?

fields.label: Must Include
fields.help: What TWO things must I explain or specify?

fields.label: Boundary
fields.help: Who receives it? What day is constrained?

fields.label: Task Commitment Note
fields.help: I need to write a message that ...

cycleB.prompt: Send a message to a classmate asking them to help prepare a class charity stall. Include the date and two materials to bring.
cycleB.question: Which is the BEST BEGINNING? None of the options is a complete finished message.

options.text: Hi Lan, could you help prepare our class charity stall this Friday? We need two materials for the display.
options.rationale: Best beginning: audience, requested action and date align, but it still MISSING names of TWO materials. It is not a complete answer.

options.text: Last year I visited a charity market with my parents.
options.rationale: This is a past story, not a request to a classmate.

options.text: Charity events are fun and useful.
options.rationale: This is general praise without the requested action or required details.

options.text: Dear Principal, I am requesting more funding for the school library.
options.rationale: Wrong audience and unrelated action.

cycleB.instruction: Option A is only the best opening. Two specific materials must still be named in your repair.
cycleB.repairPrompt: Write one or two NEW sentences to improve A. Name two specific materials classmates should bring. If you can, briefly explain why each is useful.
cycleB.reflectionPrompt: Which required part did the best beginning still miss? How did you repair it?
cycleB.reviewerExamplesOnly: Please bring coloured paper and tape for our signs. Other feasible materials are acceptable; never require these exact words.

transfer.prompt: Write a note to the school sports captain asking to move practice to a different day. Propose one new day and give one reason.
transfer.instruction: Save a new four-part Task Map and one Task Commitment Note for this fresh prompt. Do NOT write the whole message by default.

fields.label: Task
fields.help: What action must you ask for?

fields.label: Must Include
fields.help: What new day and supporting reason must be included?

fields.label: Boundary
fields.help: Who receives the note? What contextual limits matter?

fields.label: Task Commitment Note
fields.help: Describe the action you will take for this reader.

supplemental.title: Action versus topic
supplemental.prompt: Write a poster reminding classmates to bring reusable water bottles for sports day.
supplemental.question: What is the required action?

options.text: Describe your favourite sports-day game
options.rationale: A personal description is not a reminder.

options.text: Remind classmates to bring reusable bottles
options.rationale: The verb reminding names the required action.

options.text: Explain how plastic bottles are manufactured
options.rationale: Interesting but not requested.

options.text: Write a diary about last year's sports day
options.rationale: Wrong text purpose and tense.

supplemental.title: Recipient versus setting
supplemental.prompt: Email the eco-club leader asking permission to hold a seed-swap table after school.
supplemental.question: Who is the intended recipient?

options.text: The whole town
options.rationale: The prompt specifies a named role, not a public audience.

options.text: The sports coach
options.rationale: Different school role.

options.text: The eco-club leader
options.rationale: The person named after Email receives the message.

options.text: The seed-swap table
options.rationale: A table is the subject of the request, not a reader.

supplemental.title: Required versus interesting details
supplemental.prompt: Send your friend a picnic invitation. State the meeting place and what food each person should bring.
supplemental.question: Which details must your message include?

options.text: Meeting place and food to bring
options.rationale: Both details are explicitly requested.

options.text: Your favourite colour and school subject
options.rationale: Neither is requested.

options.text: Names of all the teachers in your school
options.rationale: Unrelated details.

options.text: An exact 150-word explanation
options.rationale: No word limit is given.

supplemental.title: Boundary and tone
supplemental.prompt: Write a polite note to your new teacher requesting a few minutes after class to ask about homework.
supplemental.question: Which opening best fits the reader and purpose?

options.text: “Yo, stop and answer me now!”
options.rationale: Tone and command are inappropriate to the request.

options.text: “My weekend was full of homework.”
options.rationale: States a fact, not a polite request.

options.text: “Dear Sir or Madam, I demand an official refund.”
options.rationale: Wrong action and unnecessarily formal audience assumption.

options.text: “Hello Ms. Hoa, could I ask you a question after class?”
options.rationale: A clear, polite request addressed to a teacher.

aiTutor.rule: Only after exact save. Review only learner-authored Task Map/repair/transfer in this Unit. Do not transmit demo text or answer keys.
aiTutor.question: Did the learner distinguish topic, communicative action, required details and recipient/day boundary? In Cycle B, were TWO materials actually named?
aiTutor.variation: Multiple wordings are valid. A phrase can have more than one defensible semantic role.
aiTutor.noGhostwriting: Quote an exact learner phrase about a genuinely missing detail and ask what materials their friend needs to bring. Do not supply the two materials or a complete model answer.
aiTutor.fallback: AI review is currently unavailable. Your draft is saved locally; you can continue editing or finish the lesson.
